ety.text: From Old French executer (French exécuter), from Latin exsecutus, past participle of exsequor (“to follow (up/through)”, particularly in the sense “to go through with a deed or punishment”), from ex- (“out”) + sequor (“to follow”).

senses.d: To kill, especially as punishment for a capital crime.
ex: There are certain states where it is lawful to execute prisoners convicted of certain crimes.
According to international treaties, it is illegal to execute prisoners of war.

senses.d: To carry out; to put into effect.
ex: Your orders have been executed, sir!
I'll execute your orders as soon as this meeting is adjourned.

senses.d: To perform.
ex: to execute a difficult piece of music brilliantly
to execute a turn in ballet

senses.d: To carry out, to perform an act; to put into effect or cause to become legally binding or valid (as a contract) by so doing.
ex: to execute a contract

senses.d: To start, launch, or run.
ex: to execute a program

senses.d: To run, usually successfully.
ex: The program executed, but data problems were discovered.

to start, launch or run software

ex: The entire machine slowed down during the execution of the virus checker.

ex: The teacher told us that the next exercise is to write an essay.
Where noyse of armes, or vew of martiall guize / Might not reuiue desire of knightly exercize.

senses.d: Activity intended to improve physical, or sometimes mental, strength and fitness.
ex: I like to do my exercises every morning before breakfast. I do calisthenics for physical exercise, and I do crosswords for mental exercise.
